Hood Heroes - épisode 10 : coach Abdel,: Hood Heroes - Episode 10: Coach Abdel, the big brother to young athletes in Saint-Michel
« Coach Abdel, c’est comme un grand frèr: “Coach Abdel is like a big brother”
« Bonjour, coach ! » Les voix des adoles: “Hi, coach!” The voices of teenagers in sportswear ring out in the large gym where their soccer practice is about to begin. One by one, the players walk past Abdel to shake his hand before heading off to get ready in their respective locker rooms.
Abdelaziz Mohamad a toujours été quelqu’: Abdelaziz Mohamad has always been athletic and upbeat. At least, that’s what the young players he has coached for the past five years think. “I’ve been with them since they were in Secondary 1. Today, I’m with them for their final year. I’ve watched them grow up,” Abdel says right off the bat.
Parmi les ballons de soccer qui s’éparpi: Amid the soccer balls scattered across the polished gym floor, La Converse joins Coach Abdel during a practice with his players. He himself walked the halls of Joseph-François-Perrault high school, and he decided to give back to his community by helping teenagers through sport.
« J’ai un parcours assez atypique, début: “I have a pretty unconventional background,” the coach begins. “I studied here, at Joseph-François-Perrault, which we call ‘JFP.’” Abdel also played for the high school’s futsal (indoor soccer) team, a few years before becoming its coach. “After that, I went to Cégep du Vieux Montréal, in social science, Individuals profile,” he continues.
Au début de l’âge adulte, Abdel fait fac: In early adulthood, Abdel faced difficulties that kept him from pursuing his studies full time. “I finished CEGEP, but I wasn’t able to continue my studies at university,” he says with regret. “I kept working, I piled up several jobs, part-time or full-time, nights as well as days. It allowed me to develop a rhythm of life.”
Abdel déclare qu’il n’a jamais eu l’inte: Abdel says he never intended to stop studying, but that life decided otherwise. “When I was young, I was faced with a lot of family problems. It wasn’t always easy: separations, arguments, there were a lot of them. I was raised in a loving family, but there were still a lot of problems at home,” he confides. He thinks for a few seconds, then continues: “It wasn’t always rosy. I went through situations with some family members that pushed me out the door.”
À peine majeur, Abdel se retrouve donc s: Barely an adult, Abdel found himself alone and had to learn to rely only on himself. “I had to take charge of my life all on my own, and it was very hard. I lived in a rented room with strangers – not even friends. At that point, I had a part-time job and I was still in school. But it didn’t last: at my age, it wasn’t easy to juggle both at the same time.”
Ces moments plus sombres n’ont cependant: Still, these darker times didn’t break Abdel. “I fought and I didn’t give up. My goal was to have a place of my own, to be independent and to stop sharing a home with other people.” After another moment of silence, Abdel explains that his determination led him to be patient and save up so he could reach his goal a few years later.
Aujourd’hui, cela fait trois ans que l’e: Today, the 25-year-old coach has been living on his own for three years. “I handle everything I have to handle by myself, I’m independent,” he says proudly.
S’il a de quoi être fier du chemin parco: Although he has reason to be proud of how far he’s come, Abdel doesn’t deny that he had to make sacrifices. “I had to put my studies on hold. Working full time didn’t allow me to go back to school,” he explains. The coach says he could have kept going to school, but doesn’t think he could have done it “properly.” “Going to school is all well and good, but getting good grades is better. I didn’t want to go to school just to do a sloppy job of my studies.”
Malgré tout, le jeune homme estime que l: Despite everything, the young man believes the interruption to his schooling is only temporary. “I’m planning to go back to school, obviously. It’s actually my goal right now. I’m working really hard so I can afford to go back the right way. I want to focus and succeed,” he says with determination.
<strong>Être un grand frère pour ses jeu: Being a big brother to his players
En plus d’être entraîneur, Abdelaziz est: Besides being a coach, Abdelaziz is also a big brother. His younger brother is now 18. “My relationship with my brother taught me a lot about young people. You don’t realize it, but when you grow up with a younger brother, you slowly get used to connecting with young people. Knowing what to say to my players helps,” he says.
Junior, Khaled et Sebastian sont trois d: Junior, Khaled and Sebastian are three members of the team Abdel coaches. The coach has watched all three grow up. In fact, it was they – and the rest of the team – who asked Abdel to keep coaching them for a fifth consecutive year, when he was thinking about taking a break. After Sunday afternoon practice, they come over to tell us about their coach.
« Coach Abdel, c’est comme un grand frèr: “Coach Abdel is like a big brother,” Junior begins. The captain of the indoor soccer team, he says his coach took him under his wing from the moment he started high school. “Not only do we learn from him because he’s good at soccer, but he also shows us that he values us beyond the sport,” the 16-year-old continues. “He’s very disciplined, and he teaches us that discipline. He gives us structure but helps us at the same time; it motivates us a lot,” he finishes.
Il est suivi par Khaled, son coéquipier,: He is followed by his teammate Khaled, who says that besides supporting them in sport, the JFP alumnus helps them in their everyday lives. “He helps me a lot to have confidence in myself and to dare. At first it was in sport, but growing up with him pushed me to become more confident in other aspects of my life,” he explains, still a bit out of breath from the workout he just finished.
Pour sa part, Sebastian connaît Abdel de: Sebastian, for his part, has known Abdel since Secondary 1. Now a graduating student, he sees his coach as someone he can trust. “He showed me that he believed in me. It helped me on the field, but even more off it. He’s an incredible person, generous, kind, funny,” he lists off in his high school’s locker room.
« Quand ils entrent sur le terrain, j’ap: “When they step onto the field, I teach my players that there are things they can do and things they can’t. That they have teammates out there and they have to value each other like brothers. That they can’t mistreat each other, that they have to help and motivate each other. It’s the same thing in society,” the coach lists.
Prévenir ces problèmes passe par l’inter: Preventing these problems means intervening with young people, says the Saint-Michel coach. “If we prepare young people and surround them with support, they’ll be better able to react to those influences. We can really limit and reduce the damage outside. I think a young person who’s focused, who has a good head on their shoulders, who’s well surrounded and who has good values won’t easily be influenced or drawn into dark situations,” he says.
Pour ce qui est de l’entraînement, il es: As for coaching, he believes he does his intervention work with young people through sport. “We often forget it, but sport pushes young people to become very disciplined. If you want to keep playing, you have to be at least a bit organized and punctual: qualities you need in adulthood,” he says. Beyond discipline, soccer also has a positive effect on young people’s morale. “Personally, when I’m not feeling great, all I have to do is touch a ball and I forget everything. I know that afterward, I can bounce back, I can start over. That bad energy goes away, and it’s the same for teenagers. It’s something really special that they experience by training here,” he says, smiling.
Avec du recul, qu’il a acquis à force de: With the perspective he has gained from spending time with teenagers, Abdelaziz believes what young people lack is motivation and values. “In a neighbourhood like this one, in Saint-Michel, young people dabble in a bit of everything. When they’re at school, they have structure, they act in a more disciplined way. When they leave the school walls, they’re out there, and we can’t really control the culture outside.”
Cette « culture du dehors » est une réfé: This “culture outside” refers to what happens on the street, in the hood. That hood often has a negative connotation in Saint-Michel.
Abdel rappelle néanmoins que, lorsqu’on: Abdel nevertheless points out that when you’re a teenager, you’re very impressionable and more likely to make impulsive decisions with negative consequences. “When a 15- or 16-year-old starts something bad – related to the problems we were talking about earlier – they don’t necessarily realize what they’re doing. They don’t necessarily have a negative goal, they’re often convinced they know what they’re doing. But they don’t, and we always have to remind young people to think before acting and to think about the future,” he explains.
En terminant, Abdel souhaite passer un i: To close, Abdel wants to pass an important message on to young people: “Everything we do has repercussions on the future. Really. We need to focus on the importance of life.” A little emotional, he pauses, then goes on: “I can confirm to you that life is really fleeting. People die every day. As soon as you make a decision, you have to think about where it will lead you, who it will affect. Acting impulsively leads nowhere,” Coach Abdel concludes.
En inculquant des valeurs liées au sport: By instilling values tied to sport in his players, Abdel hopes “not only to shape athletes, but also men, future adults.” He continues, saying he wants to “raise respectful, motivated and, above all, cultured young people – who always want to keep learning,” and hopes that “the negative that comes into their lives pushes them to move forward and not backward.”
Du même souffle, il ajoute que le sport: In the same breath, he adds that sports are one solution – among others – to the problems of the street. “Young people are exposed to these problems every day, especially in neglected and disadvantaged neighbourhoods. We hear a lot about crime, gun violence, drug use and drug dealing among young people,” he begins. In his view, the problems young people face stem largely from the people around them and the environments they spend time in growing up. “Nobody’s going to wake up one fine day and decide to start dealing drugs or go buy a gun. It’s a question of influence,” he says.
